name: Astragalus
lead: Astragalus, in this entry, refers to the root of Astragalus membranaceus (also Astragalus mongholicus or A. propinquus), known in traditional Chinese medicine as huangqi.[1][2] It is a perennial legume native to temperate Asia, and the root is one of the 50 fundamental herbs of traditional Mongolian medicine and a well-known tonic in Chinese medicine.[1][2][3]

People take it as a longevity and vitality tonic: the stated chain is immune and antioxidant support, then faster recovery and healthier ageing, which shows up as better training capacity and a fresher look. Its main constituents are polysaccharides, saponins such as astragaloside IV, and isoflavones including calycosin and formononetin.[2][4] Reviews describe immune-stimulant, antioxidant, antidiabetic and anti-ageing activities, mostly from laboratory and animal work.[3][4][5][16]

Human studies include a small crossover trial in which astragaloside supplementation was followed by faster recovery after muscle-damaging exercise, and trials in kidney disease, chemotherapy fatigue and Alzheimer disease.[15][17][18][8][9] Wikipedia reports limited clinical evidence for Astragalus products.[2]
infobox: Temperate Asia: Kazakhstan, Siberia, Mongolia, western and northern China [2]

paras: In traditional Chinese medicine the root is used as a tonic, described in a 2014 review as an immune stimulant, tonic, antioxidant, hepatoprotectant, diuretic, antidiabetic, anticancer and expectorant.[3] A review of its polysaccharide fraction describes use to invigorate the spleen and replenish qi.[4] Wikipedia lists it among the fundamental herbs of traditional Mongolian medicine.[2]

A 2017 review in Aging and Disease describes A. membranaceus as a well-known Chinese tonic used for more than 2,000 years, and covers experimental work on telomerase activity, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects and vascular and brain ageing; it also mentions TA-65, a proprietary root-derived extract, in connection with immune ageing.[16]

The root contains astragaloside IV and other saponins, polysaccharides (Astragalus polysaccharide, APS) and flavonoids.[4][5][2] Reviews of astragaloside IV and of APS report anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, cardioprotective and neuroprotective effects in cell and animal models.[4][5][6] The saponin cycloastragenol, an astragaloside IV derivative, is marketed separately as a telomerase activator.[2] Chemical analyses have found that the composition of commercial Radix Astragali differs by season and from adulterant plants.[7]

A 2023 review of plant extracts as skin-care agents lists several Astragalus species among plant materials with wound-healing and photoprotective effects, for example Astragalus floccosus and Astragalus gombiformis, as part of a broad survey of botanicals for moisturising, anti-ageing and regenerative cosmetic uses.[19] These listings concern other Astragalus species in cell or laboratory settings rather than the huangqi root taken orally.[19]

Wikipedia notes that the root contains the saponin cycloastragenol, which is derived from astragaloside IV and marketed separately as a telomerase activator in anti-ageing supplements.[2] The 2017 review links telomerase activity with the root's anti-ageing research.[16]

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 11 men, astragaloside supplementation for 7 days around a muscle-damaging eccentric exercise protocol was followed by lower creatine kinase, LDH and myoglobin on days 1 to 3, suppressed IL-6 and TNF-alpha, a rise in IGF-1 during early recovery and strength returning to baseline two days sooner than with placebo.[15] This is the study most directly relevant to the recovery chain, and its sample is small.

A multicentre, assessor-blind trial in 118 Hong Kong patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease found that adding astragalus granules to standard care for 48 weeks was followed by a slower decline in eGFR (4.6 mL/min/1.73m2 per year, 95% CI 1.5 to 7.6) and 7.9 mmHg lower systolic blood pressure, with no significant difference in albuminuria.[17] A 66-patient phase 2 trial of astragalus polysaccharide in early breast cancer chemotherapy found no significant overall difference in fatigue, with less fatigue worsening in the premenopausal subgroup.[18]

Registered studies are mostly small and in medical conditions: Phase 2 trials in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease (66 and 76 participants), a Phase 2/3 trial in aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage (120), a Phase 2 study of a herbal formula for cancer fatigue (92) and a 24-person study in healthy adults examining muscle function.[8][9][10][11][12] Registry entries do not report results here, and no trial has an appearance outcome. No studies found on astragalus for facial appearance, skin or hair.

Wikipedia notes that other Astragalus species poison livestock through alkaloids, nitro compounds and accumulated selenium, and that these constituents have not been detected in A. mongholicus used in supplements and traditional preparations.[2] Selenium toxicity was first characterised in livestock grazing selenium-accumulating Astragalus species.[14] The sources consulted do not describe human adverse effects or drug interactions for the root.

card.summary: The root behind huangqi, a classic Chinese tonic herb; promoted for longevity and immunity, with no appearance trials.
card.note: Evidence is largely preclinical; other Astragalus species are toxic to livestock.

quick.overview:
Astragalus root (huangqi) is a staple tonic herb in traditional Chinese medicine, now sold as a longevity and immune-support supplement.
Reviews describe immune, antioxidant and metabolic effects, mostly from lab and animal work. Human trials are few and small, and none tests appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Its polysaccharides, astragalosides and isoflavones are reported to modulate immune signalling and inflammation in cell and animal models. Astragaloside IV is metabolised to cycloastragenol, sold separately as a telomerase activator.
quick.risks: Wikipedia states the toxic constituents of other Astragalus species were not found in the species used in supplements. Human adverse-effect data are limited; product quality and adulteration are noted in chemical analyses.

chain: Root extract taken as a daily tonic
Reported anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and immune effects; one small trial shows faster strength recovery after hard exercise
Quicker recovery, more training and a healthier, younger-looking appearance
angle.text: People use astragalus as an anti-ageing and recovery tonic, hoping for better energy, quicker bounce-back from training and healthier skin. Research is strongest as laboratory and small clinical work on inflammation, immunity and exercise recovery.
